Heavenly Session
HEV-en-lee SESH-un
n. phrase (Christology; eschatology; mediatorial kingdom)
From Latin sessio (a sitting; from sedere, to sit); in classical theology, the sessio ad dexteram Patris (session at the right hand of the Father) refers to Christ's present state of exaltation and reigning authority following His ascension. The phrase summarizes Psalm 110:1, cited by the New Testament more than any other Old Testament text: “The LORD said to my Lord, 'Sit at My right hand, till I make Your enemies Your footstool.'”

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The heavenly session of Christ is His present state of exaltation at the right hand of the Father, entered at the ascension, exercised now, and to be completed at the second coming. Psalm 110:1 — the most-quoted Old Testament verse in the New Testament — establishes the paradigm: the ascended Lord sits in the position of royal honor and authority until the Father makes all enemies His footstool. Hebrews applies this with precision: Christ, having offered one sacrifice for sins for all time, “sat down at the right hand of God” (Heb 10:12) — unlike the Old Testament priests who never sat, because their work was never finished. His session signals the completion of the atoning work. Acts 2:33 declares He was “exalted to the right hand of God” and from that position poured out the Spirit at Pentecost. Ephesians 1:20–23 places Him “at His right hand in the heavenly places, far above all rule and authority and power and dominion,” with all things subjected under His feet. Hebrews 7:25 connects the session directly to His ongoing intercessory work: He “always lives to make intercession” for those who draw near to God through Him. The session is therefore not passive rest but active reign: He governs His church through the Spirit, mediates for His people as High Priest, and extends His kingdom until every enemy is subdued under His feet. The second coming will not inaugurate His reign; it will consummate it, delivering up the kingdom to the Father (1 Cor 15:24–28). The session is the present tense of the reign of Christ.

Webster 1828 Definition

The present exaltation of the ascended Christ at the Father's right hand (Ps 110:1; Heb 10:12), from which He pours out the Spirit, intercedes for His people, and governs His kingdom — not a passive waiting but an active mediatorial reign that will be consummated at the second coming.

HEAVENLY SESSION, n. phrase (Christology; eschatology). The present state of the ascended Christ, exalted to the right hand of the Father (Acts 2:33; Eph 1:20), in which He exercises mediatorial kingship, intercedes for His people (Heb 7:25), and governs His church through the Holy Spirit. The session began at the ascension and continues until the second coming.

The theological weight of the session rests on Psalm 110:1, the most-cited Old Testament verse in the New Testament: “Sit at My right hand, till I make Your enemies Your footstool.” The verb “sit” indicates royal enthronement and its temporal clause indicates the session is not permanent in its present form but will yield to the consummate victory of the kingdom.

Hebrews uses the session to establish the finality of Christ's atonement. Old Testament priests stood continually to offer sacrifices that could never finally remove sin; Christ sat down because His one sacrifice is complete and sufficient (Heb 10:11–14). The session is the posture of finished redemptive work.

The session connects to three distinct but related activities: (1) intercession — He “always lives to make intercession” (Heb 7:25) as the believer's advocate before the Father; (2) governance — He rules His church, sends the Spirit, and extends His kingdom through the preaching of the gospel; (3) expectation — He waits in the posture of Psalm 110:1 until the Father completes the subjugation of all enemies, culminating in death itself (1 Cor 15:26).

The 1689 LBCF (8.4) confesses that after resurrection and ascension, Christ was “received into glory in heaven, where he sitteth at the right hand of God, making intercession” — the same language that ties session to intercession as the present work of the ascended Lord.

Key Scripture

Psalm 110:1 — "The LORD said to my Lord, “Sit at My right hand, till I make Your enemies Your footstool.”"

Hebrews 10:12 — "But He, having offered one sacrifice for sins for all time, sat down at the right hand of God —"

Acts 2:33 — "Therefore, having been exalted to the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, He has poured forth this which you both see and hear."

Hebrews 7:25 — "Therefore He is able also to save forever those who draw near to God through Him — since He always lives to make intercession for them."

Modern Corruption

Dispensational premillennialism has sometimes implied the kingdom is deferred or the session is merely preparatory waiting rather than active reign; this misreads the New Testament's present-tense language of Christ's royal authority exercised now through the Spirit and the church.

expand to see more

Dispensational premillennialism, especially the older Scofield-Darby variety, taught that the Davidic kingdom was offered to Israel, rejected, and “postponed” until the millennium. In this scheme, the present age is a parenthesis and Christ's session at the right hand is essentially a waiting period until He can reign from Jerusalem. This scheme conflicts directly with Acts 2:29–36, where Peter identifies the Davidic enthronement promised to David's seed (Ps 132:11) as already fulfilled in Christ's resurrection and ascension. The session is the kingdom; the enthronement is now; the footstool is being prepared, not postponed. Reformed amillennialism and postmillennialism agree on this point despite their different eschatological timelines.

A subtler corruption reduces the heavenly session to a mere status-marker — Christ is “in authority” in some abstract sense — while practically ignoring that He exercises that authority now through the Spirit's work in the church, through the preaching of the gospel, and through the intercession that sustains every believer. Hebrews 7:25 will not allow a passive session: the ascended Christ “always lives to make intercession,” and this intercession is the ground of the believer's perseverance. The session is a living, active, priestly-royal work, not a ceremonial posture.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Psalm 110:1 (the most-cited OT verse in the NT), the exaltation language of Acts 2 and Ephesians 1, and the High Priest typology of Hebrews; formally confessed in the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds as Christ sitting at the right hand of the Father, and elaborated in the 1689 LBCF and Westminster Confession as ongoing mediatorial and intercessory ministry.

expand to see more

Psalm 110:1 (The LORD to my Lord) — the foundational text; cited or alluded to in Matthew 22:44, Acts 2:34–35, Romans 8:34, 1 Corinthians 15:25, Ephesians 1:20, Hebrews 1:3, 1 Peter 3:22, and Revelation 3:21 — the most referenced OT verse in the NT, making the session the most attested element of NT Christology.

Acts 2:33–36 (Pentecost sermon) — Peter's proof that Jesus is Lord: having been exalted to the right hand of the Father and having received the Spirit, He poured out the Spirit at Pentecost; this is the evidential link between the session and the Spirit's present activity.

Hebrews 1:3, 8:1, 10:12 (High Priest at rest) — the contrast between the Levitical priests who stood and never sat (Heb 10:11) and Christ who sat because His sacrifice is finished; the session is the New Testament's signature image of completed atonement.

Creedal formula (sedet ad dexteram Patris) — the Apostles' Creed confesses He “sitteth at the right hand of God the Father Almighty”; the Nicene Creed says He “sitteth at the right hand of the Father”; this is among the oldest and most universally confessed elements of Christian theology.

1689 LBCF 8.4 — after resurrection and ascension, Christ “sitteth at the right hand of God, making intercession, and shall return”; the Confession ties session, intercession, and second coming into a single coherent narrative of Christ's mediatorial office.

Usage

"The heavenly session is the theological warrant for the church's confidence in intercessory prayer: every prayer is addressed to the Father through a Son who “always lives to make intercession” and who is “able to save forever” those who draw near through Him."

"Preaching the session corrects both presumption and despair: it corrects presumption because the kingdom is not merely ours to build — it is Christ's to govern and extend through the Spirit; it corrects despair because the kingdom is not in doubt — the Sovereign has already sat down in victory."

"The session as the Christological present tense means Christ is not absent from His church: His physical presence is at the Father's right hand, but His mediatorial presence through the Spirit is continuous, active, and governing."
